 Empty Villages 
 The disappearance of India’s villages is often discussed through the language of migration, employment and economic development.
 Statesman News Service | New Delhi | November 10, 2026 8:20 am 
 15 April 2020 
 8 mins read -->
 -->
 -->
 Photo: IANS/Representative 
 The disappearance of India’s villages is often discussed through the language of migration, employment and economic development. But behind these familiar categories lies a less visible crisis: the gradual abandonment of those who cannot leave. An ageing population, deprived of family support and essential services, is being left to confront the final years of life in communities that are steadily ceasing to exist. 
 Vinod Kapri’s film Pyre, set in Uttarakhand, brings this reality into sharp focus through the lives of an elderly couple. Their children have migrated in search of employment, neighbours have gradually departed, and the familiar network of mutual assistance has almost vanished. What remains is a landscape of extraordinary natural beauty inhabited by people for whom even ordinary survival has become increasingly difficult. The predicament is not unique to Uttarakhand. Across India’s hill districts and remote rural regions, migration has altered the social structure of entire communities. Young people leave because education, healthcare and employment opportunities are concentrated in towns and cities. 
 Advertisement
 Their departure is economically understandable, but its cumulative consequences are devastating. Agricultural traditions weaken, local institutions lose their participants, and the elderly are deprived of the social networks that once sustained them. It would be simplistic to interpret this abandonment as a moral failure of younger generations. A son who leaves his parents to earn a living elsewhere may be responding to circumstances over which he has little control. The deeper failure is institutional. Governments have repeatedly spoken of rural development without adequately addressing the concentration of economic opportunity in urban centres. 
 Advertisement 
 Connectivity, schools, medical facilities and viable employment remain unevenly distributed. Financial assistance alone cannot compensate for the absence of a functioning community. There is another uncomfortable dimension. India’s entertainment industry often struggles to accommodate films that do not conform to established commercial expectations. Pyre, despite international festival recognition and 18 awards, remained without a distributor for two years. Its eventual theatrical reception suggests that audiences are not necessarily indifferent to intimate, socially relevant storytelling. 
 The reluctance of commercial gatekeepers may reveal more about their assumptions than about public taste. The film’s larger significance, however, lies in the questions it raises about development and responsibility. Appeals to young people to remain in their ancestral villages will achieve little unless governments create conditions in which staying is sustainable. Decentralised employment, accessible healthcare, reliable transport and educational opportunities must become integral to rural policy rather than recurring electoral promises. A village should not have to retain its elderly inhabitants merely as custodians of a disappearing past. 
 Nor should growing old mean being left without assistance because the next generation has been compelled to seek opportunity elsewhere. The ultimate measure of development is not how many people leave rural India for a better life, but whether those who remain can live with dignity. When even the prospect of a dignified death becomes uncertain, the failure is considerably greater than rural depopulation. It is a failure of society itself.
